name: Archetype: infantry armies with limited mechanisation (1914-1945)

weightNotes.aggression: Mostly defensive postures by smaller states facing larger industrial neighbours (Poland 1939, Yugoslavia and Greece 1941, China 1937-45), with local offensives. Middle-low.
weightNotes.maneuver: Foot infantry and horse-drawn artillery move at marching pace; mechanised formations were absent or a handful of brigades (House ch. 3-4). Low.
weightNotes.flanking: Horse cavalry and light infantry could still envelop in forests and broken terrain (Finnish motti tactics at Suomussalmi 1939-40) but not against motorised enemies. Low-moderate.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Defended cities, fortified lines and border regions for political and economic reasons (Poland covered the Corridor, Poznan and Silesian industry; DA Pam 20-255 part one). Moderate.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Cordon deployments along long frontiers left thin reserves that could not reach a breach in time (Poland 1939; House ch. 4). Low-moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Horse cavalry, few aircraft and scarce radios; the German attack was a tactical surprise to the Polish army despite known concentrations (DA Pam 20-255 ch. 6). Low.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Basis: share of starting strength lost (killed, wounded, captured, missing) at the moment of withdrawal or break, never the battle total with pursuit. derived:breakpoint-quartile: modelRules.breakpoint.loserCasualtyShareAtBreak.worldwars mid 0.152, grade C. No source gives an archetype-specific share at withdrawal; previous 0.25 was a judgment. Era baseline.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Few tanks, little antitank capacity, scarce radios and almost no close air support (House ch. 3-4); artillery-infantry cooperation at First World War standard.
weightNotes.initiative: Mostly centralised command on the First World War model; varies by army (Finnish small-unit initiative was high). Low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Rail- and horse-bound supply kept operations close to railheads; consumption was low, so foot armies could keep going on short rations. Middle.

summary: Conscript infantry armies of 1914-1945 that lacked the industry for large-scale mechanisation: rifle divisions marching on foot, artillery and supply drawn by horses, horse cavalry for reconnaissance, a few tank battalions and a small air force. They fought on First World War lines: entrenched linear defence along frontiers or rivers, deliberate infantry-artillery attacks, and withdrawal by rail and road. Examples: the Polish army of 1939, the Yugoslav, Greek and Romanian armies, the Chinese National Revolutionary Army, and the Finnish army of the Winter War.
whyItWorked: On terrain that denied mechanised forces (forest, mountains, marsh, winter) and against road-bound enemies, cheap infantry held well and could even win: Finnish motti encirclements at Suomussalmi (1939-40), Greek mountain fighting against Italy (1940-41), Chinese defence and the Taierzhuang victory (1938). Low consumption made these armies durable on poor logistics.
whereItFailed: Against mechanised, air-supported opponents in open country they were outmanoeuvred and encircled: Poland 1939 (cordon defence on the frontier, broken in days; DA Pam 20-255), Yugoslavia in eleven days and Greece in April 1941, Shanghai and Nanjing 1937, and the Romanian Third and Fourth Armies at Stalingrad in November 1942, which lacked antitank guns to stop Soviet tank corps.

sources.title: House, Towards Combined Arms Warfare (CSI Research Survey 2, 1984), ch. 3-4
Kennedy, The German Campaign in Poland (1939), DA Pamphlet 20-255
Lupfer, The Dynamics of Doctrine (Leavenworth Paper 4, DTIC ADA563816)
